voice.refText: You wake up and discover you can pause time. 10 seconds once a day. At first, you use it for dumb things. You catch your falling coffee. You dodge your boss in the hallway.

Lotte.describe: A low, warm female voice: a woman in her late fifties, a baker who has seen everything. Alto, slightly husky, unhurried and dry, a hint of a German accent. Speaks plainly, close to the listener.

Jonas.describe: A relaxed male baritone: a man of about thirty, the listener's flatmate. Young, warm and a little husky, quick and playful, easy laughter under the words, casual modern English.

Frau Weber.describe: A sharp, bright female voice: a woman in her sixties on a city tram. Slightly nasal mezzo, quick and indignant, a voice that carries down the whole carriage.

Mehmet.describe: A flat, tired male baritone: a tram driver in his forties. Gravelly, bored and matter-of-fact, speaking over his shoulder like a public announcement.

Herr Brandt.describe: A thin, precise male baritone: a bank officer in his fifties. Slightly nasal, polite and measured, every word chosen, a quiet clerk's restraint.

Karl.describe: A deep, gravelly male bass: a delivery man in his forties who hauls flour sacks. Big, gruff, loud and blunt, a working man's voice from the back of a van.

lines.text: Day thirty-one. Ten million euros, pouring off your phone.
lines.say: [thrilled, fast, a grin, the hook said like a dare] Day thirty-one. Ten million euros, pouring off your phone.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day fifty-five. More money than the whole planet makes in a year.
lines.say: [bigger, awed, building, almost laughing at the size of it] Day fifty-five. More money than the whole planet makes in a year.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And it starts with one cent. And a card that says no.
lines.say: [sudden drop to dry and close, a smirk, the punchline] And it starts with one cent. And a card that says no.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Declined.
lines.say: [dry, deadpan, eyes on the red light of the card reader, a baker who has seen everything] Declined.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: One cent? That's your whole account?
lines.say: [leaning over your shoulder, reading the screen aloud, dry disbelief, half a laugh held back] One cent? That's your whole account?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: My treat. Again.
lines.say: [warm, teasing, coins already on the counter, a running joke between flatmates] My treat. Again.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: Did your phone just... rip?
lines.say: [groggy, alarmed, whispered too loud, sitting up in the dark] Did your phone just... rip?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: Two cents. Don't spend it all at once.
lines.say: [sleepy sarcasm, flat, the coat already going back over his head] Two cents. Don't spend it all at once.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Two cents. Last night, one. You know that.
lines.say: [hushed, close to the mic, the first words of the narrator, a secret shared in the dark] Two cents. Last night, one. You know that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You always know the number.
lines.say: [warm, slow, a fact about a friend, a small smile] You always know the number.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: What if your money doubled every day?
lines.say: [curious, lifting, the question asked plainly to you, eyes wide] What if your money doubled every day?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every night. Whatever's there at midnight, twice by morning. From one cent. And it will not stop.
lines.say: [steady, building, each clause a step, the last four words cold and even] Every night. Whatever's there at midnight, twice by morning. From one cent. And it will not stop.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's the rule, once. At midnight, whatever's in your account doubles. New money. Taken from no one, the rule says.
lines.say: [clear, matter-of-fact, a teacher who likes you, a faint doubt on 'the rule says'] Here's the rule, once. At midnight, whatever's in your account doubles. New money. Taken from no one, the rule says.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: There is no off switch. Except one. Exactly zero at midnight. Not a cent more. Not a cent less.
lines.say: [lowered, deliberate, slow, a finger raised, slowing on 'exactly zero', the last two sentences even and quiet, a rule, not a warning] There is no off switch. Except one. Exactly zero at midnight. Not a cent more. Not a cent less.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Two cents. You laugh. You spend nothing. And Jonas buys the rolls, like every morning.
lines.say: [light, amused at you, a chuckle under 'nothing', the last clause warm and easy] Two cents. You laugh. You spend nothing. And Jonas buys the rolls, like every morning.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte doesn't laugh.
lines.say: [quiet, a small turn, the smile gone] Lotte doesn't laugh.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: My grandfather's story. The king's wheat.
lines.say: [low, tender, remembering, setting grains down one by one as she speaks] My grandfather's story. The king's wheat.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: A king, a chessboard. One grain on the first square, and double on every square after. By the last square, the board owes more wheat than the whole world grows in over a thousand years.
lines.say: [storytelling, hushed, patient at the start, a widening awe toward the end, no hype] A king, a chessboard. One grain on the first square, and double on every square after. By the last square, the board owes more wheat than the whole world grows in over a thousand years.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But you're counting squares. The money's counting nights.
lines.say: [dry, cold, a turn of the head, the second sentence slower] But you're counting squares. The money's counting nights.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day eleven. Ten euros. You've waited for this one.
lines.say: [bright, expectant, a little grin, the drum roll before a small moment] Day eleven. Ten euros. You've waited for this one.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: One forty. All counted?
lines.say: [brisk, unimpressed, palm out, exactly the same as every other morning, clear words] One forty. All counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Lotte. Lotte! Look who paid.
lines.say: [delighted, mock-astonished, tugging her sleeve, a stage whisper] Lotte. Lotte! Look who paid.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: I saw.
lines.say: [flat, two words, writing on the board, not looking up] I saw.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Three years. Lottery?
lines.say: [teasing, warm, narrowing his eyes at you, a real question under the joke] Three years. Lottery?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Day eighteen. Thirteen hundred euros. Jonas's birthday is Saturday. You order a cake.
lines.say: [cheerful, quick, a plan forming, pleased with yourself] Day eighteen. Thirteen hundred euros. Jonas's birthday is Saturday. You order a cake.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day nineteen. Twenty-six hundred. You add a band.
lines.say: [giddy, a notch faster, the grin widening] Day nineteen. Twenty-six hundred. You add a band.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day twenty-one. Ten thousand. You add the street, and you stop, because you've run out of street.
lines.say: [gleeful, almost laughing, tumbling forward, a comic stop on 'run out of street'] Day twenty-one. Ten thousand. You add the street, and you stop, because you've run out of street.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Who are all these people?
lines.say: [bewildered, in pyjamas, blinking at the street, half asleep] Who are all these people?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Your party.
lines.say: [dry, arms folded behind a wall of cakes, exhausted and amused] Your party.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: I said a small cake.
lines.say: [protesting, a little hurt, pointing at nothing] I said a small cake.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Your friend ordered thirty-one. Last night.
lines.say: [flat, a nod at you, the blame placed neatly] Your friend ordered thirty-one. Last night.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: I'm thirty-one!
lines.say: [outraged and touched at once, loud, a laugh breaking through] I'm thirty-one!
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Sixty-two cakes.
lines.say: [deadpan, wiping her hands] Sixty-two cakes.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Did you count the candles?
lines.say: [softening, a knife in a cake, a smile he tries to hide] Did you count the candles?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Counts everything, that one.
lines.say: [fond, quiet, the family joke handed back, almost tender] Counts everything, that one.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Every morning you planned the party with that morning's number. Every morning the number had moved on without you. That's how a cake turns into a brass band.
lines.say: [amused, explaining, a wink in the voice, the last sentence landing like a punchline] Every morning you planned the party with that morning's number. Every morning the number had moved on without you. That's how a cake turns into a brass band.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Frau Weber: Who's paying for all this?
lines.say: [suspicious, shopping bags in both hands, loud enough for the whole tram] Who's paying for all this?
lines.speaker: Frau Weber

lines.text: Mehmet: That one, by the door. Everyone rides free today.
lines.say: [bored, over the shoulder, a public announcement with no feeling in it] That one, by the door. Everyone rides free today.
lines.speaker: Mehmet

lines.text: Frau Weber: Well. I'm staying on, then.
lines.say: [decided, settling into her seat, bags on her lap, pleased with herself] Well. I'm staying on, then.
lines.speaker: Frau Weber

lines.text: Thirty people ride to the end of the line and back. Because it's free. The whole tram, all day, costs less than tonight will hand you back before breakfast.
lines.say: [wry, fond of people, a chuckle on 'because it's free', the last clause a little dizzy] Thirty people ride to the end of the line and back. Because it's free. The whole tram, all day, costs less than tonight will hand you back before breakfast.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But here's the problem. The party was a month's money. You thought. By the morning after, it was one night's worth.
lines.say: [uneasy, slowing, a cloud over the fun, 'you thought' set apart with a small wince] But here's the problem. The party was a month's money. You thought. By the morning after, it was one night's worth.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ask people to carry on a doubling, and most guess far too low. You just did. In public. With a band.
lines.say: [embarrassed on your behalf, dry, the last three fragments each a small jab] Ask people to carry on a doubling, and most guess far too low. You just did. In public. With a band.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Each new night is worth more than every night before it, put together. So you weren't a little behind. You were living in the wrong week.
lines.say: [sober, careful, letting the arithmetic sink in, the last sentence quiet and a little frightening] Each new night is worth more than every night before it, put together. So you weren't a little behind. You were living in the wrong week.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The number's ahead of you now. You can't catch it. But the bank can. It calls.
lines.say: [tense, low, a chase you are losing, the last two words clipped like a phone ringing] The number's ahead of you now. You can't catch it. But the bank can. It calls.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Herr Brandt: Where does it come from?
lines.say: [polite, careful, pen poised, a man who already knows you will not have an answer] Where does it come from?
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Herr Brandt: Mine. Right.
lines.say: [flat, repeating it back as he writes, not believing a word of it] Mine. Right.
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Herr Brandt: If it's a mistake, we can take it back. All of it. Tonight.
lines.say: [neutral, procedural, a door left open on purpose, 'all of it' slightly weighted] If it's a mistake, we can take it back. All of it. Tonight.
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Herr Brandt: Is it a mistake?
lines.say: [quiet, direct, looking at you over his glasses, a real question] Is it a mistake?
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Herr Brandt: Not a mistake. Signed.
lines.say: [satisfied, precise, the stamp coming down on 'signed', filing it away] Not a mistake. Signed.
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Day twenty-eight. One point three million. You buy the building. The bakery, the flats, the lot. Lotte never pays rent again.
lines.say: [warm, generous, proud of you, a breath of relief on the last sentence] Day twenty-eight. One point three million. You buy the building. The bakery, the flats, the lot. Lotte never pays rent again.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Yesterday's. Free.
lines.say: [gruff and kind, two words, clear, no ceremony, the deed already forgotten] Yesterday's. Free.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Lotte: Morning. All counted?
lines.say: [cheerful, routine, palm out, chalk in the other hand; two clear words after 'Morning', a question rising on 'counted'] Morning. All counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: You hold the phone up to her. And the number won't fit.
lines.say: [quiet, then stopping short, a catch in the breath on 'won't fit'] You hold the phone up to her. And the number won't fit.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ten million euros. Say it the other way. A billion. Cents.
lines.say: [awed, slow, each number weighed, a disbelieving half-laugh on 'cents'] Ten million euros. Say it the other way. A billion. Cents.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Is that... all yours?
lines.say: [stunned, small, a loop of paper in his fingers, a joke he cannot find] Is that... all yours?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: First, the obvious trick. Take it all out in cash. The machine gives you five hundred euros. Move it to another bank? Still your money. It doubles there too.
lines.say: [quick, conspiratorial, a clever plan, then flat comic deflation on 'five hundred euros'; 'Still your money' a shrug, the last line deadpan] First, the obvious trick. Take it all out in cash. The machine gives you five hundred euros. Move it to another bank? Still your money. It doubles there too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So you spend. Faster than it grows. Can you?
lines.say: [playful, a challenge, quick] So you spend. Faster than it grows. Can you?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-one, before midnight. A car. A penthouse. A tiny jet. Four million, gone by dinner.
lines.say: [fast montage energy, ticking items off, gleeful, 'tiny jet' with a laugh] Day thirty-one, before midnight. A car. A penthouse. A tiny jet. Four million, gone by dinner.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: At midnight, what's left doubles anyway. Thirteen million. You shopped all day, and woke up richer.
lines.say: [comic deflation, deadpan, the last clause a punchline] At midnight, what's left doubles anyway. Thirteen million. You shopped all day, and woke up richer.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-three. Forty million euros. Jonas has a football club. Not supports. Has. The one at the end of the tram line, that loses every Saturday.
lines.say: [delighted, comic, the correction 'not supports, has' sharp and proud, fond on the losing] Day thirty-three. Forty million euros. Jonas has a football club. Not supports. Has. The one at the end of the tram line, that loses every Saturday.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: You bought my club.
lines.say: [dazed, flat, a statement he has to say out loud to believe] You bought my club.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: They're winning.
lines.say: [alarmed, standing, as if reporting a fire] They're winning.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: I don't know what to do with my hands when they win.
lines.say: [lost, comic, looking at his own hands, a man whose world has changed shape] I don't know what to do with my hands when they win.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: You're thinking it. Why not just invest it?
lines.say: [knowing, straight to the viewer, a raised eyebrow] You're thinking it. Why not just invest it?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You try. You buy shares. The price shoots up. Because you're the one buying. Now you're richer twice.
lines.say: [quick, building, then a comic beat on 'richer twice', exasperated and amused] You try. You buy shares. The price shoots up. Because you're the one buying. Now you're richer twice.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Investing is for making money grow. You have the opposite problem.
lines.say: [dry, clear, a wink in the voice on 'the opposite problem'] Investing is for making money grow. You have the opposite problem.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-five. A hundred and seventy million. Jonas has a new idea: Lotte's rolls, delivered to the whole city. By drone. A thousand drones. You pay.
lines.say: [excited, quick, the idea growing as it goes, 'A thousand drones' big, 'You pay' dry] Day thirty-five. A hundred and seventy million. Jonas has a new idea: Lotte's rolls, delivered to the whole city. By drone. A thousand drones. You pay.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Bread from the sky! They order on the app, we drop it on their roof.
lines.say: [thrilled, selling it, waving the phone, a man with his first business] Bread from the sky! They order on the app, we drop it on their roof.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: And who bakes it?
lines.say: [flat, arms folded in her doorway, one eyebrow up] And who bakes it?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: You do. Look. Forty orders. A hundred!
lines.say: [delighted, not listening, reading the phone as it pings, louder on 'a hundred'] You do. Look. Forty orders. A hundred!
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: I have two hands and one oven. Eighty rolls a morning. I bake what I bake.
lines.say: [calm, firm, counting it out for a child, the last sentence final] I have two hands and one oven. Eighty rolls a morning. I bake what I bake.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: A thousand drones take off. Eighty of them carry a roll. Forty thousand orders.
lines.say: [spectacle, then comic arithmetic, each number landing harder, the last one a punchline] A thousand drones take off. Eighty of them carry a roll. Forty thousand orders.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-seven. You stop reading the number before you spend. It makes no difference. Every morning, more than you started with.
lines.say: [tired, the fun gone flat, a treadmill in the voice, the last sentence heavy] Day thirty-seven. You stop reading the number before you spend. It makes no difference. Every morning, more than you started with.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's what you'd believed. Money is a pile of stuff. More money, more stuff.
lines.say: [gentle, patient, laying out the wrong idea without mockery] Here's what you'd believed. Money is a pile of stuff. More money, more stuff.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It isn't. Money is a ticket for things people make. And Lotte's oven makes eighty rolls a morning. No more. Your pile is a bigger ticket for the same bread.
lines.say: [clear, firm, the correction landing plainly, warmth on Lotte's name, 'No more.' flat and final, the last sentence slow] It isn't. Money is a ticket for things people make. And Lotte's oven makes eighty rolls a morning. No more. Your pile is a bigger ticket for the same bread.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But everything you spend has to land somewhere. And it lands where you stand.
lines.say: [ominous, low, the second sentence quieter than the first, a door closing] But everything you spend has to land somewhere. And it lands where you stand.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Karl: Same flour. New price. Triple.
lines.say: [blunt, invoice held out, no apology, the last word dropped like a sack] Same flour. New price. Triple.
lines.speaker: Karl

lines.text: Lotte: Triple? Karl, it's the same sack as last month.
lines.say: [shocked, then indignant, pointing at the sack, an old friend's tone] Triple? Karl, it's the same sack as last month.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Karl: Same sack. But the whole street has money now. Your friend upstairs pays for everything.
lines.say: [patient, hard, a man who has done his sums, a nod up at your window on 'upstairs'] Same sack. But the whole street has money now. Your friend upstairs pays for everything.
lines.speaker: Karl

lines.text: Karl: So the mill charges more. The farmer charges more. Everyone does.
lines.say: [matter-of-fact, clear and plain, every word distinct, ticking them off on his fingers, not unkind] So the mill charges more. The farmer charges more. Everyone does.
lines.speaker: Karl

lines.text: Lotte: And I charge more for rolls.
lines.say: [quiet, working it out, the anger draining into something worse] And I charge more for rolls.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Karl: Everyone does.
lines.say: [softer, lifting the sack off the van, almost sorry] Everyone does.
lines.speaker: Karl

lines.text: Day forty. Prices rise first where the new money lands. Your street. One forty. Two ten. Three euros. Four twenty.
lines.say: [slow, clear, explaining one hard thing, the numbers falling one by one like chalk] Day forty. Prices rise first where the new money lands. Your street. One forty. Two ten. Three euros. Four twenty.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: She counts what her savings will buy. Last month, a year of flour. Tonight, four months. She didn't spend a cent.
lines.say: [hushed, aching, slow on 'half a year', the last sentence almost a whisper] She counts what her savings will buy. Last month, a year of flour. Tonight, four months. She didn't spend a cent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: A third.
lines.say: [barely voiced, one word, the pencil stopped, looking up at the framed note] A third.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: It isn't taken from anyone. Except it is. From everyone. A little. Every night.
lines.say: [the turn: quiet, confessional, each fragment heavier, 'every night' almost broken] It isn't taken from anyone. Except it is. From everyone. A little. Every night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So you try the obvious thing. You give it away. Day fifty. Five trillion. A million euros to every phone in Berlin.
lines.say: [bold, bright, a big plan, rising to 'every phone in Berlin'] So you try the obvious thing. You give it away. Day fifty. Five trillion. A million euros to every phone in Berlin.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Flour. Not money.
lines.say: [firm, kind, pushing the envelope back, a rule of her own] Flour. Not money.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Nobody goes to work. Why would you? And by Saturday, a roll costs sixty-three euros. Because every million was new money. Chasing the same rolls.
lines.say: [comic, quick, 'Why would you?' a shrug, then clear and firm on the reason] Nobody goes to work. Why would you? And by Saturday, a roll costs sixty-three euros. Because every million was new money. Chasing the same rolls.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: This has happened before. For real. In 1324, a king from Mali, Mansa Musa, gave away so much gold in Cairo that gold stayed cheap there for at least twelve years. Your gifts do it to bread. Ask Jonas.
lines.say: [storytelling, leaning in, 'for real' quiet and certain, a little wonder on the gold, then dry and quick on the last two sentences] This has happened before. For real. In thirteen twenty-four, a king from Mali, Mansa Musa, gave away so much gold in Cairo that gold stayed cheap there for at least twelve years. Your gifts do it to bread. Ask Jonas.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Sixty-three? Since when?
lines.say: [outraged, comic, counting his coins again, clear words] Sixty-three? Since when?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Since that one.
lines.say: [quiet, not unkind, a nod at you, the truth said once] Since that one.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Not me.
lines.say: [gentle, immovable, two words, shaking his head at the phone] Not me.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: Then it's me making the rolls cost that. I'd rather owe you one.
lines.say: [soft, steady, a man explaining himself for once, a small smile at the end] Then it's me making the rolls cost that. I'd rather owe you one.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Day fifty-two. You're on the news. One account in Berlin, growing faster than anyone can count.
lines.say: [bright, quick, a grin, the world finally noticing, 'faster than anyone can count' rolling out] Day fifty-two. You're on the news. One account in Berlin, growing faster than anyone can count.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day fifty-five. The number passes what the whole world makes in a year. Every loaf, every car, every hour of work on Earth. About 128 trillion dollars.
lines.say: [awed and afraid, slow, the list building, the figure said plainly, no hype] Day fifty-five. The number passes what the whole world makes in a year. Every loaf, every car, every hour of work on Earth. About a hundred and twenty-eight trillion dollars.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You have more than that. Above a bakery. And tomorrow is twice this.
lines.say: [hushed, absurd and terrible, a dry breath on 'above a bakery', the last sentence cold] You have more than that. Above a bakery. And tomorrow is twice this.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Never hit zero, and by day two hundred and sixty-seven your account holds more cents than the estimated number of hydrogen atoms in the observable universe.
lines.say: [hushed awe turning to urgency, slowing on the number, 'cents' crisp with its t, the last words wide and quiet] Never hit zero, and by day two hundred and sixty-seven your account holds more cents than the estimated number of hydrogen atoms in the observable universe.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And there's only one way out. Exactly zero, at midnight.
lines.say: [low, a thread pulled tight, the rule coming back, slow and quiet on 'exactly zero'] And there's only one way out. Exactly zero, at midnight.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You call Herr Brandt. Now. The universe can wait. Berlin can't.
lines.say: [decided, fast, a breath before 'now'; the last two sentences a dry joke, quick] You call Herr Brandt. Now. The universe can wait. Berlin can't.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Herr Brandt: So it was a mistake.
lines.say: [quiet, on speaker, a statement and a question, no triumph in it] So it was a mistake.
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Herr Brandt: Everything goes. Your wages as well. You understand?
lines.say: [careful, slower, a man making sure, clear words, a touch of pity on 'your wages as well'] Everything goes. Your wages as well. You understand?
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Herr Brandt: Fifty minutes.
lines.say: [brisk, procedural, the keyboard already going] Fifty minutes.
lines.speaker: Herr Brandt

lines.text: Zero. Everything. Your wages, your savings, three years of roll money. Ten minutes to midnight. You breathe out.
lines.say: [drained, relieved, the list quiet and even, a real exhale on the last three words] Zero. Everything. Your wages, your savings, three years of roll money. Ten minutes to midnight. You breathe out.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then the phone buzzes. A refund. From the tram app. From the day you paid for the whole tram. One cent.
lines.say: [alarmed, sharp, the fun of the tram turned to dread, 'one cent' small and terrible] Then the phone buzzes. A refund. From the tram app. From the day you paid for the whole tram. One cent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: One cent at midnight is two. Two is four. And it all starts again. Three minutes.
lines.say: [panicked, fast, the doubling heard as a clock, the last two words urgent] One cent at midnight is two. Two is four. And it all starts again. Three minutes.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Who takes one cent, at three minutes to midnight? The machine wants a euro. The tram is still free. Jonas is asleep.
lines.say: [breathless, running, urgent and funny, each failure faster] Who takes one cent, at three minutes to midnight? The machine wants a euro. The tram is still free. Jonas is asleep.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: All counted?
lines.say: [tired, warm, through a door opened a hand's width, the gag one last time, almost a kindness, clear words] All counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: You count. One cent. Into her palm. Twenty-three fifty-nine and fifty-eight.
lines.say: [tense, quick, then slowing on the time, every word clear, a held breath] You count. One cent. Into her palm. Twenty-three fifty-nine and fifty-eight.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Zero, doubled, is zero.
lines.say: [quiet, complete, after the silence, a thing finally true, no music] Zero, doubled, is zero.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Counted.
lines.say: [deadpan, dry, one word, the smallest smile, the gag's last return] Counted.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Day fifty-six. Jonas pays. He always pays.
lines.say: [morning, plain, a small smile, back where we began] Day fifty-six. Jonas pays. He always pays.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A coin isn't a thing. It's Lotte, agreeing to bake tomorrow.
lines.say: [quiet, clear, the one idea to take home, said as a complete thought, warmth on her name] A coin isn't a thing. It's Lotte, agreeing to bake tomorrow.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then Jonas's phone rips.
lines.say: [sudden, low, a cliffhanger sting] Then Jonas's phone rips.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Did my phone just... rip?
lines.say: [stunned, staring at his own screen, whispered too loud] Did my phone just... rip?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Be honest. If one cent started doubling in your account tonight, which day would you stop it? Tell us the day in the comments. And subscribe. Jonas might need you.
lines.say: [direct, friendly, lighter, leaning toward you, the question real and easy to answer; the last sentence a small knowing smile, no hype] Be honest. If one cent started doubling in your account tonight, which day would you stop it? Tell us the day in the comments. And subscribe. Jonas might need you.
lines.speaker: narrator
